::: {.lead}
Before Byte Bay submits a game, the producer asks: "Will it pass the
review?" The answer is in the stores' guidelines. Today there are no new
ideas: you use what Lecture 9 taught and read the guidelines like a
reviewer. You find their main parts, you judge why games are rejected, and
you build your own pre-submission checklist. Do each activity alone. The
results of the activities are at the end of this worksheet: try first, then
compare.
:::

## Recall

- Publishing has six steps: account, build, listing, rating and privacy,
  review, release.
- The **app review** checks every game and update against the store's
  **guidelines**.
- Common reasons for a rejection: crashes, an incomplete build ("coming
  soon"), a misleading listing, a missing privacy policy.
- A **staged rollout** gives a new version to a small part of the players
  first.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Recall"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="the players|the price"}
What does the app review check a game against?
:   the store's guidelines

    Why: The review checks every new build against the store's rules.

The listing shows screenshots of another game. What will the review say?
:   misleading listing

    Why: The screenshots must show the real game.

Which step comes right before the release?
:   the review

    Why: The store checks the game before it goes live.
:::
:::

## Activity 1 · The main parts of the guidelines

Apple's **App Review Guidelines** have five parts; the **Google Play
Developer Policy** covers the same topics in its own order.

- **Safety:** objectionable content, children, chat and user content.
- **Performance:** a complete build without crashes, a true listing.
- **Business:** in-app purchases, ads, loot boxes and their odds.
- **Design:** no copies or spam, enough features.
- **Legal:** privacy and data, intellectual property.

![The main parts of the store guidelines.](images/guideline-parts.png){width=90%}

{{< sim file="sims/guideline-sorter.html" poster="sims/guideline-sorter.png" title="Guideline Sorter: which part of the rules?" height="520" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
Old summaries on other websites may be wrong today: the stores change the
rules several times a year. Read the official page and write its date.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 1 · Find the parts · 10 min"}
1. Open the official App Review Guidelines (developer.apple.com) or the
   Google Play Developer Policy Center. Write the title and the date of the
   page, and find the part about in-app purchases.
2. In **Guideline Sorter**, sort all nine problems.

*Your product:* the title and date of the page, the name of the part about
purchases, and your score.

::: {.check}
A good answer: "App Review Guidelines, Apple Developer (with the date shown
on the page): part 3, Business, 3.1 In-App Purchase", or "Google Play
Policy Center: Monetization and Ads › Payments", with its date. In
Guideline Sorter all nine problems sorted: chat and children → Safety;
crashes and listings → Performance; purchases and loot boxes → Business;
copies → Design; privacy and licences → Legal.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Which part?"}
Choose the part of the guidelines. You can use an answer more than once.

::: {.match extra="Weather|Music"}
A chat between players.
:   Safety

    Why: Safety covers chat and content made by users.

Gems sold for money.
:   Business

    Why: Business covers in-app purchases and ads.

A privacy policy.
:   Legal

    Why: Legal covers privacy, data and intellectual property.

The game crashes on start.
:   Performance

    Why: Performance asks for a complete build without crashes.
:::
:::

## Activity 2 · Why was it rejected?

The rejection message names the rule that the game broke. A studio reads
the rule, fixes the problem and submits again.

- *Gem Rush* sells a mystery chest for 2 USD with random gems, and the odds
  are not shown. Part: **Business** (loot boxes). Rule: show the odds of
  each item before the purchase. Fix: an "odds" button on the chest screen.
- Six common reasons: crashes, an incomplete build, a misleading listing,
  privacy, payments outside the store or hidden odds, other people's content
  without a licence.

![Six common reasons for a rejection.](images/rejection-reasons.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 2 · Two games you know · 10 min"}
1. Choose two games you know.
2. For each one, find one rule of the guidelines that it must follow (for
   example its purchases or its chat). Write the part and the rule.

*Your product:* two games, each with a part and a rule.

::: {.check}
A good answer looks like: "A football game sells coins: Business, the
coins are sold through the store's own payment. A puzzle game has a chat:
Safety, players can report and block other players."

- ☐ Each rule fits something the game really has.
- ☐ Each rule has the right part of the guidelines.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · Why rejected?"}
Choose the reason.

::: {.match extra="the price is too low|the icon is green"}
"Coming soon" on most buttons.
:   incomplete build

    Why: The game shows features that do not exist yet.

A mystery chest without odds.
:   loot-box odds not shown

    Why: A paid random item must show its odds.

The heroes of a famous film, without a licence.
:   other people's content

    Why: Characters and brands of others need a licence.
:::
:::

## Activity 3 · A pre-submission checklist

A **pre-submission checklist** turns the guidelines into yes-or-no
questions that a studio asks before every upload:

- one line for each common reason and each part that fits the game;
- fitted to the game: a chat needs reporting and blocking; a game without
  purchases needs no loot-box line;
- checked before **every** new build.

![A pre-submission checklist for Pocket Quest.](images/checklist.png){width=90%}

::: {.callout-note title="Activity 3 · Your checklist · 12 min"}
1. Choose a game you know or plan.
2. Write a checklist of at least eight yes-or-no lines for it, and name the
   part of the guidelines for each line.

*Your product:* a checklist of eight lines with their parts.

::: {.check}
A good checklist for a game with purchases and a chat has lines like: "No
crashes on three phones? (Performance)", "Every button works, no 'coming
soon'? (Performance)", "Screenshots of the real game? (Performance)",
"Privacy policy link and data form? (Legal)", "Purchases through the store?
(Business)", "Odds of random items shown? (Business)", "Report and block in
the chat? (Safety)", "Licences for all music and art? (Legal)".

- ☐ Eight lines, each a yes-or-no question.
- ☐ Each line fits the game and names its part.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note .ai-task title="Task with AI · A checklist checked at the source"}
**Goal:** a pre-submission checklist of twelve lines for *Pocket Quest* (a
chat, gems for money, a mystery chest), in which every line points to the
official rule. By hand this takes long; the AI drafts, and you check.

1. **Ask the AI:** start with this prompt.

   ::: {.prompt}
   Make a pre-submission checklist of 12 yes-or-no questions for a mobile
   game with a chat between players, gems sold for money and a mystery
   chest with random items. For each question, name the part of Apple's App
   Review Guidelines that it comes from.
   :::

2. **Do it yourself:** open the official App Review Guidelines and find
   each rule. Next to each line write the number of the rule (for example
   3.1.1) and the date of the page. Remove lines that are not rules, and add
   any line that is missing.
3. **Check:** the line about the mystery chest must say that the odds are
   shown before the purchase; the chat line must have reporting and
   blocking. If the AI names a rule you cannot find, mark it.

*Your product:* the checked checklist, and one sentence on what the AI got
wrong or what you changed.

::: {.check}
A good product has twelve yes-or-no lines; each with a rule number from the
official page (for example 1.2 user-generated content for the chat, 3.1.1
in-app purchase for the gems, 3.1.1 odds for the mystery chest, 5.1 privacy)
and the date of the page; and one sentence such as "The AI gave a wrong
rule number for the chat, so I took 1.2 from the page."

- ☐ Every line points to a rule you found yourself.
- ☐ The odds line and the chat line are there.
:::
:::

## Case study: Review Board

Today Rami plays the reviewer. Six games wait: *Pocket Quest 1.0*, tested
and complete; *Sky Farm*, with "coming soon" buttons and an empty shop;
*Gem Rush*, with a mystery chest and no odds; *Hero Wars X*, with the heroes
of a famous film series; *Tiny Chat Pets*, a game for children with free
chat; and *Speed Car 3*, which crashes on start. The Game challenge of the
interactive page uses these games. In the mini-game below you decide for
each one.

## Exercises

1. Name the five parts of Apple's App Review Guidelines.
2. Which part covers a chat between players? And the purchase of gems?
3. Why read the official page and not a summary?
4. Name three common reasons for a rejection.
5. What must a game with loot boxes show?
6. What is a pre-submission checklist, and when is it checked?
7. A game uses the music of a famous band without a licence. Which part,
   and what is the fix?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Safety, Performance, Business, Design, Legal.
2. Safety; Business.
3. The rules change several times a year.
4. For example crashes, an incomplete build, a misleading listing.
5. The odds of each item, before the purchase.
6. Yes-or-no questions from the guidelines, checked before every upload.
7. Legal (intellectual property); a licence, or music the studio owns.
:::
